title: Trade Liberalization, Exit, and Productivity Improvements: Evidence from Chilean Plants
research_question: Does exposure to foreign competition through trade liberalization improve manufacturing plant productivity, and if so, do gains arise primarily from within-plant efficiency improvements or from the reallocation of output and resources from less to more efficient producers (including the exit of inefficient plants)?
data_description: The paper uses an unbalanced plant-level panel from the census of Chilean manufacturing plants employing ten or more workers, collected by Chile's National Institute of Statistics, covering 1979-1986. The unit of observation is a plant (over 90% are single-plant establishments), with 4,379 plants and 25,491 plant-year observations. Key variables include gross output, value added, intermediate materials, skilled and unskilled labor (number of employees), capital stock (constructed via perpetual inventory using 1980/1981 book values), and investment, all expressed in constant 1980 pesos. Plants are classified at the four-digit ISIC level into export-oriented (exports >15% of output), import-competing (imports >15% of domestic output), or nontraded sectors using trade data from the U.N. Yearbook of International Trade Statistics and Statistics Canada. Industry tariff data come from the Chilean Central Bank, and real effective exchange rates from the IMF.
institutional_context: Chile undertook one of the most dramatic trade liberalizations of the developing world between 1974 and 1979, eliminating most non-tariff barriers and reducing tariffs that frequently exceeded 100% in 1974 to a uniform 10% ad valorem rate across all manufacturing industries by 1979. Apart from a temporary tariff increase during the 1982-1983 recession (peaking at a uniform 35% in 1984 before falling to 20% by mid-1985), Chile maintained its commitment to free trade throughout the 1980s, and tariffs remained uniform across manufacturing sectors. This drastic and broad-based opening exposed previously sheltered domestic producers to substantial foreign competition and was accompanied by massive plant turnover: roughly 35% of plants active in 1979 had ceased production by 1986, accounting for about 25% of 1979 manufacturing employment. The uniformity of tariffs across industries, combined with variation in natural exposure to trade across sectors, provides a setting to compare adjustment across import-competing, export-oriented, and nontraded plants.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Trade liberalization led to productivity improvements in Chilean manufacturing plants.
